newsitem.title: UK: IMF gold sales could rely on U.S Congress - official.
newsitem.headline: IMF gold sales could rely on U.S Congress - official.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund's (IMF) proposed sale of five million ounces of gold from its reserves would ultimately come down to the U.S. Congress giving the go-ahead, the IMF's treasurer said on Tuesday.

Commenting on the proposed sale at the fifth Central Banking Conference, David Wiliams said "it was a done deal" the gold would be sold if the IMF failed to raise the proceeds of the sale by other means.
"But to achieve the sale would require an 85 percent majority and the executive director from the U.S. would need Congressional permission before he could vote," Williams said.
The United States controls 18 percent of the vote.
The IMF needs the money for interim financing of its Enhanced Structural Adjust Fund (ESAF) which was set up to provide debt relief help for around 20 of the world's poorest nations.
"The gap in the financing could be filled not by gold sales but by further borrowing by the ESAF trust or from the IMF's own resources at market-related prices," Williams said.

He said if the IMF raised the financing now it would have to need about 1.3 billion special drawing rights (SDRs) but by the time the backing was actually required the total would have swollen to $2.50 billion SDRs or $3.30 billion.

The facility could be raised by contributions from the IMF members. "The members agreed to contribute more (about 1 billion SDRs) for 2000-2004. If that is not sufficient, then gold would be sold up to 5 million ounces. That is a done deal," he said.
However he added that "we are hardly talking 1997 (for the sale) given we will be waiting for the Congress."

The gap in financing the ESAF will occur if the IMF is to continue to offer the poorest countries financing over a five-ten year term at 1/2 percent per annum in return for stringently enforced balance of payment adjustment programmes.
The ESAF was established after the first sale of IMF gold when 50 million ounces were sold between 1976 and 1980, he said.
He said five million ounces represented about five percent of annual gold supply, eight percent of annual gold mine output and 60 percent of estimated daily market turnover.
Selling 500,000 ounces per sale which WIlliams envisaged, would amount to about seven percent of daily market turnover.
When the IMF sold gold before 25 million ounces was sold through the market and 25 million ounces restituted back to its members raising $4.50 billion.
"The IMF did not suffer any credibility loss," he said.
After 2004, profits from the original gold sale come through to allow continued financing, he added.
